title: Synchronization: One after another!
concept: An accident occurs when multiple threads enter a shared resource (such as a bathroom stall) at the same time. What is needed at this time is a ‘lock (synchronized)’.

steps.title: Start main method
steps.explanation:
**`public static void main(String[] args)`**

This is the program entry point.
Create a bank account and start your mission.

steps.title: Create account object
steps.explanation:
Creates a `BankAccount` object to be used as a shared resource.
This object has an invisible ‘monitor lock (key)’ inside.

steps.title: synchronized method
steps.explanation:
If `synchronized` is added in front of a method, the thread trying to execute this method must obtain the key of the corresponding object (`account`) to enter.
Only one thread can execute this method at a time.

steps.title: Critical Section
steps.explanation:
Only the thread that holds the key can safely change `balance`.
Other threads will have to wait outside until this task is finished.
This area of ​​code where only one thread must execute at a time is called a 'critical area'.

quiz.question: How many locks can a Java object have?
quiz.explanation:
Every object in Java has only one 'monitor lock'.
So only one thread can enter the synchronized area at a time.

misconceptions.wrong: The more synchronized you use, the faster the program becomes.
misconceptions.correct: no! Synchronization actually reduces performance because it lines up threads.
misconceptions.why:
This is because waiting time occurs.
You should use it minimally and only on absolutely necessary shared resources.

keyTakeaway: synchronized is a ‘shield that protects data from being distorted.’ Remember, there is only one key per object!
